newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia's parliament vote on PM.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia's parliament vote on PM.

text.p: Slovenia's parliament started voting on Wednesday on whether to back the candidacy of acting Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek to form the next government.
The voting began at 11 a.m. (1000 GMT), a parliamentary official said.
President Milan Kucan last week called on Drnovsek, leader of the centre-left Liberal Democrats, to try to form an administration after inconclusive elections on November 10.
The Liberal Democrats won most votes in Slovenia's second general election since independence from former Yugoslavia, but look unlikely to win enough support in parliament.
Drnovsek, 46, whose party won 25 of the 90 parliamentary seats, can only count on at best another 20 seats, one short of an absolute majority.

The assembly appeared equally split between between parties, including the former communists, which say they will back Drnovsek, and an alliance of rightwing parties which together won 45 seats in the election -- also one short of an absolute majority.
"I expect...the outcome will be very tight," Drnovsek told national radio on Tuesday afternoon.
Drnovsek this week signed cooperation agreements with Desus, a party representing pensioners, and the United List of Social Democrats, the former communist party.
He has also won support from the Nationalist Party and is expected to receive the votes of two representatives of the Hungarian and Italian minorities, securing 45 votes.
He said he has not managed to secure support of any of the rightwing parties belonging to the so-called "Spring" alliance, saying none were prepared to negotiate.

The alliance, comprising the conservative People's Party, the centre-right Social Democrats and the Christian Democrats, has remained more united since the election than political observers had forecast.

The right is pressing for People's Party leader Marjan Podobnik, 36, to be called by Kucan to form the next government. But Podobnik may also fail to win the extra one vote to secure a majority in a second parliamentary vote.
Social Democrats on Tuesday accused the Liberal Democrats of trying to bribe one of their deputies into voting for Drnovsek, but the Liberal Democrats denied the allegations.

"I do not believe Drnovsek will get enough support today, but Podobnik's chances in the second round are no better," Drago Zajc, a professor of politics at the Ljubljana University's Faculty of Social Sciences, told Reuters.
"However, I expect someone will be elected in the third round as parliamentary members will try to avoid early elections," Zajc added.

In the first two rounds, parliament has to elect a prime minister with an absolute majority, while in a third round a relative majority is sufficient. If all three votes are unsuccessful, the president may have to call early elections.
